title: Index: The Observable Universe at Scale
description: The observable universe spans about 93 billion light-years across and holds an estimated two trillion galaxies — the part of the universe light has had time to reach us from since the Big Bang. Beyond that particle horizon, space continues; we simply cannot see it. This record is the index's top-level scale card: every distance, count, and age below hangs off these numbers.

title: Index: The Cosmic Distance Ladder
description: Astronomers measure the universe one rung at a time: parallax for nearby stars, Cepheid variables' period-luminosity relation for nearby galaxies, Type Ia supernovae as standard candles for the far field, and redshift for the deep cosmos. Each rung calibrates the next, and the whole ladder's current tension — the Hubble constant disagrees between early- and late-universe measures — is the biggest open problem in cosmology. Every distance in this index cites its rung.

title: Index: The Standard Model Particle Census
description: All known matter and forces reduce to 17 fundamental particles: 6 quarks, 6 leptons, 4 force carriers, and the Higgs boson. The up/down quarks and the electron build every atom; the rest appear in cosmic rays, colliders, and the early universe. This record is the index's particle table — the complete roster as of 2026, with the honest note that neutrinos' masses and dark matter's identity remain open.

title: Index: The Fundamental Constants
description: A handful of numbers set the universe's operating parameters: the speed of light c, the gravitational constant G, Planck's constant h, the fine-structure constant α ≈ 1/137, and a few more. Change α by a few percent and stars, chemistry, and life fail. Since 2019 the SI units are defined by fixing several of these constants exactly — the universe's source code, pinned. This record tables the index's canonical values.

title: Index: The Stellar Life Cycle
description: Stars are mass-sorted destinies: below 0.5 solar masses, red dwarfs burn for trillions of years; Sun-like stars become red giants then white dwarfs; above 8 solar masses, supernovae leave neutron stars; above ~20–25, black holes. Every heavy atom in your body was forged in these furnaces or their explosions. The index files each stage with its mass range, endpoint, and remnant — the complete stellar biography in one table.

title: Index: Galaxy Classification — The Hubble Sequence
description: Hubble's tuning fork still organizes galaxies: ellipticals (E0–E7, round to flattened), spirals (Sa–Sc, tight to loose arms), barred spirals (SBa–SBc), and irregulars that fit nowhere. The Milky Way is a barred spiral, SBbc; Andromeda a classic spiral. Modern surveys add dwarf galaxies by the thousands and merger remnants, but the fork remains the index's top-level galaxy key.

title: Index: Black Hole Archetypes
description: Black holes come in three confirmed sizes: stellar-mass (3–100 suns, from collapsed stars, seen in X-ray binaries and LIGO mergers), intermediate (hundreds to thousands of suns, still elusive), and supermassive (millions to billions, anchoring every large galaxy — Sagittarius A* at 4.3 million, M87* at 6.5 billion, both imaged). Primordial black holes remain hypothetical. The index files each class with its formation channel and best-observed example.

title: Index: Exoplanet Detection Methods
description: Over 5,500 exoplanets are catalogued, found five ways: transits (brightness dips — Kepler's haul), radial velocity (stellar wobble — 51 Pegasi b), direct imaging (young hot giants), microlensing (distant cold worlds), and astrometry (positional wobble). Each method has a bias — transits favor close-in planets, imaging favors far-out giants — so the true census is inferred, not seen. The index cross-references every method with its discoveries and blind spots.

title: Index: The Cosmic Web
description: Galaxies are not scattered — they trace a web of filaments millions of light-years long, with galaxy clusters at the nodes and vast voids between. Dark matter scaffolding, mapped by weak lensing, underlies the visible web; the Sloan Digital Sky Survey and DESI charted millions of galaxies to reveal it. This record is the index's large-scale-structure entry: the universe's architecture at the grandest scale.

title: Index: Dark Matter Evidence
description: Dark matter is the most evidenced unseen thing in science: galaxy rotation curves stay flat where visible mass predicts a fall (Rubin, 1970s), the Bullet Cluster shows lensing mass separated from hot gas, and the cosmic microwave background's ripples demand ~27% of the universe be cold dark matter. What it IS — WIMPs, axions, primordial black holes — remains unknown after decades of direct detection. The index files the evidence as established and the identity as open.

title: Index: Dark Energy Evidence
description: In 1998 two supernova teams found the universe's expansion is accelerating — distant Type Ia supernovae are dimmer than a decelerating universe allows. The CMB and galaxy clustering agree: ~68% of the cosmic budget is dark energy, mathematically a cosmological constant to current precision. Whether it is vacuum energy (with its infamous 10^120 discrepancy) or new physics is the deepest open question in the index.

title: Index: The Cosmic Microwave Background
description: The CMB is the afterglow of the Big Bang: released 380,000 years in when atoms formed and light finally traveled freely, now redshifted to microwaves at 2.725 K from every direction. Its one-part-in-100,000 temperature ripples are the seeds of all structure, and their pattern nails down the universe's age, composition, and geometry. COBE, WMAP, and Planck mapped it with increasing precision — the index's most precise dataset.

title: Index: Big Bang Nucleosynthesis
description: In the first three minutes, the universe was a fusion reactor: protons and neutrons fused into deuterium, helium-3, helium-4 (~25% by mass), and trace lithium — then expansion cooled it below fusion and the recipe froze. Every star since has only seasoned this primordial mix. The predicted abundances match observations to percent precision, making BBN the Big Bang's earliest directly tested prediction. The index files the full reaction network.

title: Index: The Solar System Census
description: Eight planets, five recognized dwarf planets, ~1 million known asteroids, ~3,700 known comets, and four giant-planet moon systems with nearly 300 moons between them. The census is complete for large bodies and wildly incomplete for small ones — new moons of Saturn and Jupiter are still found yearly. This record is the index's home-system entry, the best-mapped planetary system in existence.

title: Index: The Habitability Checklist
description: Habitability is a checklist, not a guarantee: liquid-water temperature range, an atmosphere thick enough to hold it, a magnetic field or thick air to blunt radiation, and energy plus chemistry for metabolism. The habitable zone — where a planet's equilibrium temperature allows surface water — is only the first filter; Venus and Mars sit near it and failed differently. The index scores candidate worlds against the full list.

fields.note: habitable zone is necessary, not sufficient
